Where do you think you’d want to apply this to? Is the increased latency tradeoff okay? Also keep in mind new DoS vectors as potential issues. "Where do you think you’d want to apply this to?" for transactions, at the p2p level - I personally don't see any issues with the increased latency if I get more privacy in return Yeah, increased latency is fine for transactions for certain use cases. Are the transactions encrypted between hops in the initial distribution phase? In other words, Can relays see the transaction? I would like to combine this with mixnets like nym to have it onion-encrypted through the mixnet Then the potential issue is DoS vectors, as relays now use resources (bandwidth) for opaque values. Does this have to live in the core EL clients? Could this be a sidecar that does the mixnet/relay and “disperses” the final value by sending it to its local EL client. > Does this have to live in the core EL clients? Could this be a sidecar that does the mixnet/relay and “disperses” the final value by sending it to its local EL client. That's where I need feedback from you guys - trying to understand the complexity around this as simplicity is still the endgoal always My opinion, make this a sidecar. It can always be merged into core later. one concern is that the sidecar must not become a single point of failure (just a quick thought now) Not sure I follow. How is different than the non-sidecar approach? I mean if the sidecar goes down and you design the EL to tolerate sidecar failure it's fine; but endgoal should be privacy be default and only "obfuscated" txs should be allowed to propagate or in other words: we don't allow any leaks Some use cases might want lower latency txs than what this can provide. Agree if the intent is to obfuscate, it should not leak. that should happen by design. I see in the Dandelion++ paper they are speaking of dandalion epochs "in the order of 10 minutes". That clearly does not fit all of our use cases, and goes against our efforts to reduce inclusion times and finality. "when its internal clock reaches some threshold" - the question is if we can tweak this in a smart way for our use cases I admit I'm not too familiar with Dandelion++, but I see some signs that makes me suspicios. - The paper I'm seeing cites only very few works, while the literature on PETs is wast and goes way back in time. - It also admittedly changes many fundamental parts of Dandelion, because of "simplifying assumptions made in Dandelion ... can lead to serious deanonymization attacks". What makes then Dandelion a good basis at all? - While the abstract appeared in Sigmetrics, which is a good sign, I don't see a full paper going through peer review, which is not a good sign in anonymity research. And, then, there are papers like this: https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.11860 I did not go through this second one, but it states "we model Dandelion, Dandelion++ and Lightning Network. We study different configurations and demonstrate that none of them offers acceptable anonymity to their users" Before going down that rabbit hole, I would take a critical look at what's the right basis to use. Correction, now I've found the full paper. It already seems much more serious 🙂 As for combining with onion encryption: one problem I see is that onion encryption requires source routing on the overlay (source routing means the source decides the whole path, there are no routing decision along the path, as e.g. in Tor). I might be wrong, but I don't think that combines well with the forwarding policies in Dendalion++. This is interesting: https://github.com/vacp2p/research/issues/119 They looked into Dandelion++ for Waku (Monero uses Dandelion++ since 5 years, so need to look into their implementation a bit) Note that all my comments apply to any anonymity protocol. I'm personally not familiar with Dandelion++ specifically, but the points should apply to any protocol we choose. I can imagine a combination dandelion shuffle and source routing, where at the end of the shuffle you add one more source routing hop that enables onion encryption.

excerpts.author: cskiraly
excerpts.content:
I admit I'm not too familiar with Dandelion++, but I see some signs that makes me suspicios.
- The paper I'm seeing cites only very few works, while the literature on PETs is wast and goes way back in time.
- It also admittedly changes many fundamental parts of Dandelion, because of "simplifying assumptions made in Dandelion ... can lead to serious deanonymization attacks". What makes then Dandelion a good basis at all?
- While the abstract appeared in Sigmetrics, which is a good sign, I don't see a full paper going through peer review, which is not a good sign in anonymity research.

And, then, there are papers like this: https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.11860
 I did not go through this second one, but it states "we model Dandelion, Dandelion++ and Lightning Network. We study different configurations and demonstrate that none of them offers acceptable anonymity to their users"

Before going down that rabbit hole, I would take a critical look at what's the right basis to use.
